soil-found-048.q: Which three elements make up most of the dry weight of plant debris, and how much of it?
soil-found-048.a: Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen, which together make up about 92% of the dry weight.

soil-found-017.q: How does plant species diversity tend to change across the soil pH range, and why?
soil-found-017.a: It tends to increase from pH 3.5 toward pH 9, because there are more calcicole species, which prefer lime-rich soils, than calcifuge species, which prefer acid ones.

soil-form-147.q: Why does limestone erode into karst landscapes?
soil-form-147.a: It is partly soluble, especially in acid: water and organic acid from the soil slowly widen its joints over thousands or millions of years, dissolving the calcium carbonate into pavements, caves and gorges.

soil-form-103.q: What materials make up superficial deposits, and how do they usually lie onshore?
soil-form-103.a: Mostly gravel, sand, silt and clay, forming relatively thin, often discontinuous patches.

soil-form-107.q: How did periglacial loess come to be deposited?
soil-form-107.a: As meltwater dwindled each autumn and winter, bare floodplains dried and wind winnowed their glacially ground silt and clay, depositing it downwind.

soil-form-008.q: What is bioturbation in the A horizon?
soil-form-008.a: The mixing of organic matter into the mineral matter by burrowing animals.

soil-form-118.q: Besides a mollic epipedon, what must a Mollisol have, and where are Mollisols common?
soil-form-118.a: A base saturation above 50%; they are common in grasslands.

soil-form-125.q: How does primary succession differ from secondary succession?
soil-form-125.a: Primary succession colonizes new surfaces with no life, such as bare rock, lava flows or freshly exposed till; secondary succession follows a disturbance.

soil-phys-001.a: How individual particles clump, bind and aggregate, which in turn sets the pattern of pores between them.

soil-phys-030.q: How does gilgai form in Vertisols?
soil-phys-030.a: Repeated shrinking and swelling churns the soil and heaves underlying material to the surface.

soil-phys-118.q: What kind of fluid is quicksand, and how does it respond to stress?
soil-phys-118.a: A shear-thinning non-Newtonian fluid: undisturbed it looks solid, but a change in stress of less than 1% suddenly lowers its viscosity.

soil-phys-099.q: How does heavy rain affect slope stability through matric suction?
soil-phys-099.a: Raising infiltration lowers matric suction along the soil water characteristic curve, cutting the soil's shear strength and slope stability.

soil-phys-175.q: How does recreational trampling change alpine soils?
soil-phys-175.a: It raises bulk density and lowers porosity, altering soil moisture and temperature and increasing runoff and erosion.

soil-water-156.q: Over what suction range does saturated flow occur, and what drives it?
soil-water-156.a: Between 0 and 33 kPa suction, up to field capacity, with gravity and differences in water pressure pushing water away from where it was applied.

soil-water-195.q: How is hydraulic conductivity found in a constant-head test?
soil-water-195.a: The volume of water passing in a set time is measured, and K follows by rearranging Darcy's law with the specimen's length, cross-section and head.

soil-water-176.q: What do the parameters α and n describe in the van Genuchten model?
soil-water-176.a: α relates to the inverse of the air-entry suction, and n, greater than 1, measures the pore-size distribution.

soil-water-157.q: By how much can tree roots raise infiltration rates through preferential flow?
soil-water-157.a: Up to 27 times, because living or dead roots open preferential channels for rainwater.

soil-phys-202.q: How do confined aquifers store water, and how large are their storativities?
soil-phys-202.a: By matrix expansion and water compressibility, with storativities far below 0.01 and as low as 10−5.

soil-phys-200.q: When was fluorescein first developed, and what is its sodium salt called?
soil-phys-200.a: In 1871; its sodium salt is uranine, and both remain among the best dye tracers.

soil-phys-160.q: How large are frost boils, and where do they occur?
soil-phys-160.a: Typically 1 to 3 metres across, in periglacial or alpine areas with permafrost.

soil-chem-187.q: Who derived the Goldich dissolution series, and when?
soil-chem-187.a: S. S. Goldich, in 1938, after studying soil profiles and their parent rocks.

soil-chem-095.q: How does vermiculite form from biotite or phlogopite?
soil-chem-095.a: By weathering or hydrothermal alteration: the micas lose the potassium between their sheets, which is replaced by magnesium and iron.

soil-chem-158.q: What are the two fates of growing agglomerates during particle aggregation?
soil-chem-158.a: They settle out as sediment, or in concentrated suspensions link into a colloidal gel.

soil-chem-102.q: Which minerals are products sold as fuller's earth usually made of?

soil-chem-051.q: Which exchanger cations are frequently used to measure cation-exchange capacity?

soil-chem-177.q: Name some substances in soil that can act as electron donors.
soil-chem-177.a: Soil organic matter, petroleum hydrocarbons, less chlorinated solvents such as vinyl chloride, and reduced inorganic compounds.

soil-chem-005.q: Which nitrogen fertilizers do not acidify the soil?
soil-chem-005.a: Nitrate sources with little or no ammonium, such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium nitrate.

soil-chem-033.q: How is net acidity calculated in acid base accounting?
soil-chem-033.a: Potential sulfidic acidity plus titratable actual acidity plus retained acidity, minus the acid neutralising capacity, in mol H+ per tonne of dry soil.

soil-bio-044.q: Which earthworms are usually used in vermicomposting?
soil-bio-044.a: The brandling worm Eisenia fetida or Eisenia andrei, which live in manure heaps rather than soil.

soil-bio-013.q: How do soil algae survive below the surface, out of the light?
soil-bio-013.a: Given steady temperature and moisture, they feed heterotrophically on easy carbon sources such as glucose.

soil-bio-229.q: Why do many northern forests of North America have a deep detritus layer that invasive earthworms can disrupt?
soil-bio-229.a: Most northern forests lost their native earthworms to the Wisconsin glaciation, so a deep detritus layer is typical and many native plants rely on it.

soil-bio-214.q: How much soil do small burrowers such as ants, termites and earthworms move worldwide?
soil-bio-214.a: So much that the global total matches the global rate of tectonic uplift.

soil-bio-187.q: Which way do roots move water during drought in hydraulic redistribution?
soil-bio-187.a: Groundwater is drawn up the taproot and released from the lateral roots into the dry surface soil; under flooding, roots move water the other way.

soil-bio-176.q: Where do ericoid mycorrhizal fungi trade nutrients with the plant, and how long do these sites last?
soil-bio-176.a: In coils inside the epidermal cells of fine hair roots, where soil nutrients are traded for plant sugars; the coils work for only a few weeks before degrading.

soil-bio-246.q: Which genera of mycorrhiza helper bacteria are most commonly reported?
soil-bio-246.a: Pseudomonas and Streptomyces; Bacillus is another.

soil-bio-093.q: Why has much humus persisted for more than 100 years?
soil-bio-093.a: It is hidden inside small soil aggregates or tightly sorbed or complexed to clays, out of reach of microbes and enzymes.

soil-bio-098.q: On what substrates do tangel and mor humus each develop in cold, humid mountains?
soil-bio-098.a: Tangel develops on alkaline substrates and mor on acidic ones.

soil-bio-256.q: What reaction does acid phosphatase catalyse, and at what pH does it work best?
soil-bio-256.a: It hydrolyses a phosphate monoester with water to give an alcohol and phosphate, at an optimum pH below 7.

soil-class-003.q: Why are natural soil classes useful?
soil-class-003.a: Experience shows that natural classes, based on morphology, behaviour or genesis, can be interpreted for many different uses.

soil-class-014.q: Why do soils on river flood plains stay azonal, or immature?
soil-class-014.a: New alluvium arrives every year, so the soils stay immature even though the farmland is fertile.

soil-class-112.q: How does soil climate differ between well-drained and waterlogged soils?
soil-class-112.a: In well-drained soils it is a subdued version of the regional climate; in waterlogged soils it depends more on local groundwater than on the atmosphere.

soil-class-135.q: On what materials and under what vegetation do Phaeozems form?
soil-class-135.a: On loess and glacial till under humid and sub-humid tall-grass steppe.

soil-class-156.q: Why do conditions in the acrotelm swing between aerobic and anaerobic?
soil-class-156.a: Its lower boundary usually coincides with the lowest level of the water table, which fluctuates within it.

soil-fert-185.q: What carbon-to-nitrogen ratio do composting microbes prefer in their feedstock?

soil-fert-232.q: At what pH range is the least soil phosphorus bound up?

soil-fert-218.q: Which paper is counted a milestone of biogeochemistry?
soil-fert-218.a: An 1844 paper by Dumas and Boussingault.

soil-fert-012.q: What share of fertilizers is applied as solids, and which are most common?
soil-fert-012.a: About 90%, most commonly urea, diammonium phosphate and potassium chloride.

soil-fert-092.q: How fast did Tukey and Wittwer find leaf-sprayed nutrients moving through the plant?
soil-fert-092.a: About one foot per hour, tracing radioactive phosphorus and potassium sprayed on leaves in the 1950s at Michigan State.

soil-fert-045.q: What proportion of biosolids is organic matter?

soil-fert-210.q: How did Peru treat guano from 1840, and what did that mean for its finances?
soil-fert-210.a: Peru made guano an exclusive state resource, and its royalties became the country's largest source of revenue.

soil-water-086.q: What three conditions cause surface runoff to form?
soil-water-086.a: Water cannot infiltrate fast enough because the soil is saturated, rain arrives faster than it can be absorbed, or surfaces are impervious.

soil-water-011.q: What is the main climatic control on water erosion?
soil-water-011.a: The amount and intensity of precipitation, especially when the soil surface lacks plant cover.

soil-water-044.q: What erosion index does the Conservation Reserve Program require land to have?

soil-water-071.q: Why does quick clay lose so much strength once remolded?
soil-water-071.a: Its clay particle structure is highly unstable, so it keeps far less strength than it had on first loading.

soil-water-028.q: Which structures carry water safely down to a gully floor?
soil-water-028.a: Drop structures, pipe structures, grass chutes and rock chutes.

soil-water-097.q: When are gabions chosen over riprap for river bank protection?
soil-water-097.a: On steep banks where flow is too fast for riprap; gabions are stone-filled wire boxes.

soil-water-263.q: How does a riparian zone protect water?
soil-water-263.a: It acts as a natural biofilter, shielding water from excess sediment, polluted surface runoff and erosion.

soil-water-259.q: What decides whether a wetland carries aquatic, marsh or swamp vegetation?
soil-water-259.a: How long flooding or groundwater saturation lasts.

soil-agri-016.q: What is Low Energy Precision Application (LEPA) in centre pivot irrigation?
soil-agri-016.a: Hanging drop heads just above the crop, or dragging hoses that wet the ground directly, to limit evaporation.

soil-fert-208.q: What forms of nitrogen are most commonly supplied by fertigation?
soil-fert-208.a: Anhydrous ammonia, ammonium nitrate or urea; nitrogen is the most common nutrient supplied.

soil-agri-003.q: Whose 1974 concept is considered the foundation of modern agroecology?
soil-agri-003.a: Harper's 1974 concept of agroecosystems, perhaps inspired by Tansley's process ecology of the 1930s.

soil-agri-125.q: For several soils, how does the optimum water content for tillage relate to the plastic limit?
soil-agri-125.a: The optimum equals 0.9 times the lower plastic limit.

soil-agri-081.q: According to the traditional theory, how do lynchets form?
soil-agri-081.a: Long ploughing makes soil slip downslope, building a positive lynchet where the surface rises and a negative lynchet where it drops.

soil-agri-088.a: It has the soil quality, growing season and moisture supply to give economically sustained high yields under acceptable farming methods, including water management.

soil-meth-029.q: What role does gas chromatography play in the Dumas nitrogen method?
soil-meth-029.a: The method ends with a gas chromatography column that separates nitrogen from carbon dioxide and water.

soil-meth-008.q: What does geomorphometry extract from digital elevation models?
soil-meth-008.a: Surface parameters and objects such as watersheds, stream networks and landforms.

soil-env-161.q: What did preliminary 2011 analyses estimate permafrost emissions to be, and what could they not account for?
soil-env-161.a: Around 15% of human emissions, but they could not account for abrupt thaw.

soil-env-269.q: What share of Earth's land do forests now cover, and how does that compare with before agriculture spread?
soil-env-269.a: About 31%, one-third less than before agriculture spread, with half that loss in the last century.

soil-env-075.q: What is Sahel drought now thought to stem from mainly?
soil-env-075.a: Rainfall variability set by sea surface temperatures, which are driven by natural variability, sulphate aerosols and greenhouse gases.

soil-env-313.q: Why did rangeland management develop in the United States?
soil-env-313.a: In response to rangeland deterioration from overgrazing and misuse of arid lands, shown by the Dust Bowl.

soil-env-037.q: What are the main mechanisms of phytoremediation?
soil-env-037.a: Phytoextraction, phytostabilization, phytovolatilization and phytofiltration, along with breakdown of pollutants by plants and by root-zone microbes.

soil-env-047.q: Which two migrations drive electrokinetic remediation, and which dominates?
soil-env-047.a: Electromigration (electrophoresis) of charged particles, the dominant one, and electro-osmotic flow of pore fluid running the opposite way.

soil-env-241.q: What limit does the WHO recommend for arsenic in drinking water, and why is it often unattainable?
soil-env-241.a: 10 μg/L; it is often unattainable in problem areas because arsenic is hard to remove.

soil-env-243.q: Above what fluoride concentration can groundwater cause dental fluorosis?

soil-env-263.q: How does the Raymond process circulate groundwater?
soil-env-263.a: Groundwater is pumped up downstream, infused with nutrients and oxygen, and re-injected upstream in a loop.

soil-env-297.q: What caused Keshan disease across its belt of China, and when did it peak?
soil-env-297.a: Selenium-deficient soil; it peaked in 1960–1970, killing thousands.

soil-hist-126.q: How is an age calculated in thermoluminescence dating?
soil-hist-126.a: The dose measured by heating is divided by the yearly dose rate, found from uranium, thorium and potassium contents plus cosmic rays.

soil-hist-100.q: How did non-reversible ploughs build ridge and furrow?
soil-hist-100.a: They turned soil toward the centre of the same strip each year, gradually building a ridge with a furrow between strips.

soil-hist-033.q: Who extended Darwin's idea of bioturbation to ants and trees, and when?

soil-hist-009.q: When did Curtis F. Marbut begin developing the first formal soil classification scheme for the United States?

soil-hist-021.q: What journey does Farmers of Forty Centuries recount?
soil-hist-021.a: A nine-month tour of Asia in 1909, studying what would now be called organic farming or sustainable agriculture.

soil-hist-066.q: Why would clayey and organic soils have kept producing clay and organic matter on the early Earth?
soil-hist-066.a: They resist erosion, and early unicellular life would also have bound the soil.
